title_full_ar: رياض الصالحين من كلام سيد المرسلين ﷺ
subject: hadith
summary: Riyad al-Saliheen ('Gardens of the Righteous') is one of the most widely read hadith anthologies in the Islamic world, compiled by Imam Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (631–676 AH / 1233–1277 CE). It brings together approximately 1,900 hadith from the Qur'an and the six canonical collections alongside other sources, organised around themes of personal piety, ethics, and righteous conduct.
overview:
Imam Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi was born in Nawa, Syria in 631 AH and died there in 676 AH at the age of forty-four. Despite his short life, he produced a body of scholarship that has remained foundational to the Islamic tradition: his commentary on Sahih Muslim (al-Minhaj), his fiqh compendium Minhaj al-Talibin (the basis of Shafi'i fiqh education for centuries), Rawdat al-Talibin, al-Adhkar, and Riyad al-Saliheen, among many others. He is almost universally referred to with the honorific Imam al-Nawawi.

Riyad al-Saliheen was composed as a practical guide to living a righteous Muslim life. Al-Nawawi's methodology was to select hadith from the recognised authoritative collections — primarily al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah, along with the Musnad of Ahmad, the Muwatta, and others — and organise them under thematic chapters addressing every aspect of a Muslim's inner and outer life. Each chapter typically opens with one or more Quranic verses on the theme before presenting the hadith.

The work is organised around approximately 372 chapters covering themes such as: sincerity (ikhlas), certainty (yaqin), patience (sabr), gratitude (shukr), truthfulness (sidq), fear of Allah (khashyah), hope (raja'), steadfastness in the face of trials, the rights of family and neighbours, manners with the learned and elders, commanding good and forbidding evil, remembrance of Allah (dhikr), supplication (du'a), and many more. The breadth of topics gives the work the character of a complete ethical manual rooted in prophetic guidance.

Al-Nawawi made the collection accessible to a general educated Muslim readership — not just scholars. He selected narrations with relatively clear meanings and presented them without extensive technical hadith commentary, though he provided brief explanatory notes where needed. This accessibility, combined with the reliability of his source selection, is the primary reason for the work's extraordinary popularity over eight centuries.

The work contains approximately 1,896 hadith in the most commonly cited editions, though counts vary slightly depending on the edition and how sub-narrations are counted. Al-Nawawi was known for his scrupulousness: where he used a hadith from al-Tirmidhi, for instance, he would note its grading in al-Tirmidhi's own terminology. He also wrote introductory notes explaining his methodology.

Major commentaries include Dalil al-Falihin by Muhammad ibn Allan al-Siddiqui al-Makki al-Shafi'i (d. 1057 AH), a detailed four-volume work; Nuzhat al-Muttaqin by Mustafa al-Khin et al. (a modern commentary in two volumes widely used in Syrian institutions); and Sharh Riyad al-Saliheen by Imam Ibn Uthaymin (d. 1421 AH), a contemporary commentary in multiple volumes that has been widely distributed.

The standard English translation is by Ezzeddin Ibrahim and Denys Johnson-Davies, published by the International Islamic Federation of Student Organisations (IIFSO), Riyadh. A more recent translation with commentary is by Nasiruddin al-Khattab (Darussalam, 2 volumes). The work has been translated into dozens of languages and is used as a foundational text in Islamic education worldwide, from madrasas to mosque study circles.

One feature that distinguishes Riyad al-Saliheen from other hadith anthologies is its integration of Quranic verses within each chapter. This approach — placing relevant ayat before or alongside the prophetic narrations on a given topic — reinforces the Quranic grounding of prophetic teaching and gives the work a devotional quality that pure hadith collections lack. Al-Nawawi's theological orientation, rooted firmly in Ahl us-Sunnah, means the work is theologically neutral across the major madhabs: it is used as a study text in Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali curricula alike. Its chapter on the remembrance of Allah (dhikr) and the chapters on du'a are among the most frequently quoted in Friday khutbahs, Islamic lectures, and private devotional practice globally. Riyad al-Saliheen is available in full on sunnah.com.
